questions.prompt: Which best describes how a large language model produces a response?
choices: It queries a database of verified facts and returns matching records
It searches the web in real time and summarizes the results
It predicts likely next words based on patterns learned from training text
It retrieves documents written by human experts and paraphrases them
questions.explanation: LLMs generate text by predicting what comes next based on patterns in training data. They do not query databases, search the web in real time, or retrieve pre-written documents.

questions.prompt: A colleague says an AI response must be accurate because it is written in a clear, professional tone with no grammatical errors. What is wrong with that reasoning?
choices: Nothing — well-formatted output is a reliable indicator of factual accuracy
Fluency and accuracy are separate things; a model can produce polished text that is factually wrong
The colleague is right for short responses but wrong for long ones
Grammar errors are actually a sign of higher accuracy because the model is being careful
questions.explanation: The model is optimized for fluent, plausible-sounding text. Fluency is independent of accuracy. A confident, well-formatted response can still be factually incorrect.

questions.prompt: You ask an AI chatbot to explain a concept from your own area of expertise and notice it gets one detail wrong. What is the most useful conclusion to draw?
choices: The tool is broken and should not be used
The error was a fluke; the tool is reliable in all other areas
AI output in your area of expertise is always wrong
AI output can contain errors even on familiar topics, and checking the things that matter is a standard practice
questions.explanation: Finding an error in a domain you know well is a healthy calibration exercise. It does not mean the tool is useless, but it confirms that verification is always warranted for claims that matter.
